notes: \cpara{Tells a joke from a collection of science jokes (footnote 1). Students asked why the near side of the plate is cool offer explanations; none says ``I don't know.''}
\cpara{Gives the punch line: the instructor had turned the plate around.}
\cpara{Asks whether a stammered ``heat conduction'' is a proper belief, which in the author's earlier posts means one that controls what you anticipate.}
\cpara{Sets ``because of heat conduction'' beside ``because of phlogiston'' and ``because of magic.''}

\cfact{Richard Feynman made the same comparison in ``Judging Books by Their Covers'' (\textsc{Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!}, 1985). Of a textbook that answered ``Energy makes it go'' for every picture, he wrote: ``Now that doesn't mean anything. Suppose it's `Wakalixes.' That's the general principle: `Wakalixes makes it go.' There's no knowledge coming in.'' The post does not mention him.}
\cpara{Grants that the two phrases differ, but says the difference is one of literary genre: Spock would say one, and Giles in \textsc{Buffy the Vampire Slayer} the other.}
\cpara{States the test: a model's substance is what it leads you to expect. ``Heat conduction'' normally predicts a warmer near side.}

\clogic{Loosely stated. Heat conduction, with the right starting condition, does explain a cooler near side. That is the physicist's answer three paragraphs later: a plate that was turned around and is ``approaching equilibrium again.'' What the student's answer lacks is a starting condition that would produce the observation. The next paragraph's ``used in such fashion'' comes closer to this.}
\cpara{Concludes that an answer which fits any outcome carries no knowledge, so the student's ``heat conduction'' is no better than ``magic.''}
\clogic{The principle is Karl Popper's, uncredited here as in ``Your Strength as a Rationalist.''}
\cstyle{Two technical terms, ``maximum entropy'' and ``anticipation-isomorphic,'' neither defined here, for a plain claim: the answer gives every outcome the same probability.}

\cpara{Describes the alternative: measure temperatures and use the diffusion equation, so that a few measurements predict the rest. The author does not say how many would be needed (``I'm not physicist enough to know'').}
\cpara{Gives the answer a physicist would reach by measuring: the plate was in equilibrium two and a half minutes ago, was turned around, and is returning to equilibrium.}
\cpara{Names the students' deeper error: they thought that saying ``because of'' followed by words from \textsc{Star Trek} was doing physics.}
\cpara{The verdict: the students moved their magic from one literary genre to another.}
\cpara{Cites the joke collection. I could not open the archived link, and I did not find the joke on Verhagen's current site.}
